10840-the-explorers-of-australia-and-the:
Ernest Favenc, himself an Australian explorer, published The Explorers of Australia and Their Life-Work in 1908 as part of the Makers of Australasia series. A portrait of Captain Charles Sturt at about fifty-four fronts the book. Companion volumes on Cook, Governor Phillip, Wakefield, and Sir George Grey were announced alongside it.

Favenc tells how explorers opened the continent, from coastal surveys to inland journeys, judging each man's work and character. His preface presents them as makers of a new nation. Readers get a readable, patriotic history of Australian exploration, written by one who knew the country firsthand.
11063-a-man-of-mark:
Anthony Hope, author of The Prisoner of Zenda, wrote this 1895 political romance about the imaginary South American republic of Aureataland. Founded in 1871 after violent turmoil, the state, nearly as big as Yorkshire, suffers under President Marcus W. Whittingham, a Virginian who moulded its constitution. A narrator, drawn into conspiracy, works upon human nature, finance, and the army.

Chapters follow a financial expedient, overtures from the opposition, a mine laid, a supper party with mixed officers, dividing the spoils, and a farewell to the country. Hope mixes adventure with satire on revolution, ambition, and diplomacy. The novel entertains readers who enjoy Ruritanian romance, with a state invented for the purpose and played for both excitement and laughs.
11128-the-red-thumb-mark:
R. Austin Freeman wrote this detective novel centred on Dr. Thorndyke, the medico-legal expert, and his friend Jervis. The story opens at King's Bench Walk, where Jervis meets his learned brother, a barrister in wig and old-fashioned dress, outside a tall brick house inscribed with the Powell arms. A suspect, a lady, confidences, and a thumbograph, an instrument for recording thumb marks, drive the plot.

Thorndyke faces a suspicious accident, an ambush, murder by post, and fingerprint experts, before playing his card at trial. Freeman, a pioneer of the scientific detective story, builds the case on forensic detail, especially the red thumb mark left at a crime scene. Readers get a fair-play mystery, where science, not guesswork, solves the crime.
11716-the-balkans-a-history-of-bulgaria-:
Nevill Forbes, Arnold J. Toynbee, D. Mitrany, and D. G. Hogarth divide this history of the Balkans by country. Forbes covers Bulgaria and Serbia, from Serbs under foreign supremacy to liberation under Kara-George and Miloš Obrenović and the two Balkan Wars.

Toynbee follows Greece from ancient to modern times, through awakening and consolidation. Mitrany covers Rumania from formation and Phanariote rule to the present war, and Hogarth covers Turkey from Osmanli origins to revolution and the Balkan War. A passage on Kapodistrias shows a police-state ideal imposed on peasants and sailors he did not know.
11923-religion-in-earnest-a-memorial-of-:
John Lyth's 1861 memorial Religion in Earnest preserves the life of his mother, Mrs. Mary Lyth of York, and is dedicated to his sister Eliza Hill, whose rare and unostentatious virtues, he writes, shed fragrance on earth but are only recorded in heaven. Lyth calls the work an act of Christian duty as well as filial affection.

The memoir draws on Mary Lyth's religious experience, presenting a Methodist woman's earnest faith as an example for readers. Its tone is intimate and devotional, concerned with prayer, duty, and daily conduct rather than with public achievement. It offers a portrait of nineteenth-century domestic piety from within a family that valued it.
13110-aunt-jane-s-nieces-at-work:
Edith Van Dyne's 1909 novel Aunt Jane's Nieces at Work sends Patricia Doyle, Beth, and their friends into local politics. Chapters run from Miss Doyle interferes and Don Quixote to a forged check, a mysterious disappearance, and returns from Fairview. Patsy, as Patricia is called, opens the tale at breakfast in her New York apartment, waving news at her father.

The nieces back Kenneth and Forbes against Hopkins, and spend money freely to win on their issue or not at all. Hopkins answers with a circular against music lessons, which Patsy calls a boomerang, since every woman at the fête now stands as an ally. The novel is a light, spirited tale of girls who take politics in hand and enjoy the fight.
13363-the-parish-clerk:
P. H. Ditchfield, writing in 1907, traces the English parish clerk from medieval days to his own time, with thirty-one illustrations. Chapters follow old choirs and parsons, the antiquity of the office, reading and singing duties, clerks in literature, smuggling days, epitaphs, and the Worshipful Company of Parish Clerks.

Long service stands out: one King's Norton clerk served sixty-two years and died in 1755 aged eighty-five, while. His successor, Henry Ford, served forty years, giving the parish a century of unbroken clerkship between them. London clerks, Clerkenwell, parish registers, sleepy churches, and women clerks complete a warm, detailed portrait of a small office that held village worship together.
14284-truxton-king-a-story-of-graustark:
George Barr McCutcheon wrote this 1909 Graustark romance, with pictures by Harrison Fisher. Truxton King, an American abroad, blunders into court plots in the hill kingdom of Graustark. A prince, a countess, and a lady in grey cross his path, and a witch's hut hides strange doings. The novel mixes love, disguise, and palace intrigue. McCutcheon tells it with high spirits and a taste for dashing scenes.

John Tullis presents King to a party where Baron Dangloss greets him like an old friend. The lady in grey smiles, blushes, and avoids his look of inquiry, while Tullis claims they know one another. An old woman at a hovel takes silver for displays of necromancy, and King crowds in to see them. Later chapters bring a bomb, a parade, a river flight, and a last stand. The tale charms as a light romance of a make-believe kingdom.
14676-women-and-war-work:
Helen Fraser's 1918 account describes how British women took up war work during the First World War, and how that work was organised. Hospitals, Red Cross units and Voluntary Aid Detachments come first, followed by huts and comforts for soldiers, munitions factories and the Women's Land Army.

Later chapters cover protection for women in industry, war savings, food production and conservation, and the wider question of woman-power replacing man-power. Fraser stresses spirit and discipline as much as output, and she does not hide pitfalls of organisation. The result is both a record of wartime labour and an argument that women's capacity had been proved beyond doubt.
14798-making-both-ends-meet-the-income-a:
Sue Ainslie Clark and Edith Wyatt study how New York working girls lived on their wages in 1911, with a dedication to Florence Kelley and a photograph by Lewis Hine. Laundry workers, shop girls and other wage earners open their budgets to the authors, item by item.

Rent, food, clothing, car fares, laundry and small pleasures are set against weekly pay, and the gap is often stark. A conference with laundrymen's associations and the Consumers' League, seeking a ten-hour day, frames the human figures. The book is social investigation at its most concrete: real incomes, real outlays, and a plain argument that wages, hours and living costs cannot be judged apart.
15147-beeton-s-book-of-needlework:
First published in Britain in 1870, Beeton's Book of Needlework teaches tatting, crochet, knitting, netting, embroidery, point lace, and Berlin work, with six hundred engravings. Each pattern states the exact amount of material needed, and each stitch is described and drawn with care. A preface by Samuel Butler fronts the book.

Monograms, initials, pillow lace, and guipure all get full treatment, so a worker can follow a design from first stitch to finish. The book served daughters of England, in its own phrase, who worked diligently with their hands. Crafters today still use it as a rich source of Victorian patterns and skill.
16074-the-definite-object-a-romance-of-n:
A New York romance by Jeffery Farnol, author of The Broad Highway and The Amateur Gentleman, issued in 1917. Farnol, a master of Regency romance, turns here to modern Manhattan. Geoffrey Ravenslee, a mournful millionaire who lacks an object, goes seeking one. A pair of whiskers opens the tale, in Farnol's jovial manner.

Ravenslee comes to Hell's Kitchen at peep of day, where Mrs. Trapes acquires a new lodger despite her elbows. Spike initiates him into the gentle art of shopping, with ankles, stairs, and neighbourliness to follow. Candies and confidences deepen the comedy. The novel delights as a rich-man-poor romance: a millionaire who finds his object in a humble street.
1626-after-dark:
Wilkie Collins's After Dark strings its stories on a single thread of interest, with Leah's Diary serving as framework for the collection. The preface explains the design, and the tales that follow, told by a travelling artist and his companions, range from Paris to Rome with mystery, love, and a touch of the macabre.

Collins takes pains to link the stories, so the book reads as a journey rather than a shelf of leftovers. The diary gives the set a personal voice. After Dark is a charming early Collins collection, and a good entry to his short fiction.
16666-carette-of-sark:
John Oxenham's 1907 novel of Sark opens with a foreword on the small, exclusive island, where forty farm holdings match those fixed by Helier de Carteret in Elizabeth's day. Chapters tell how Paul Martel fell out with Sercq and how Rachel Carre went back to her father. They tell too how two fought in the dark, and how Carette and the narrator were girl and boy together.

Oxenham dedicates the book to the Seigneur of Sark and island friends, with sixteen photographs of Sark. The tale mixes island custom, feud, and romance. Readers of Channel Island fiction will find a rich, atmospheric story of a feudal isle in modern times.
16935-thomas-henry-huxley-a-sketch-of-hi:
P. Chalmers Mitchell wrote this 1900 sketch of Thomas Henry Huxley's life and work for the Leaders in Science series, issued by Putnam's Sons in New York and London. Chapters move from school to life work, through the voyage of the Rattlesnake, floating creatures of the sea, and later public work. Huxley's path runs from Charing Cross Hospital and naval medical service to fame as a naturalist.

Mitchell tracks Huxley from student to public champion of science, with sea voyages, medusae, and Darwin debates along the way. The sketch is short, clear, and admiring without gush. It serves as a fine first life of Huxley for readers who want the man and his science in one small volume.
17173-the-bow-of-orange-ribbon-a-romance:
Amelia E. Barr's 1886 romance sets Dutch New York of long ago against love, pride, and family duty. Pictures show a heroine on steps, a knitting girl, a Dutch chair, and a love knot tied with care, while the plot moves through town houses, ships, and church life. The book is dedicated to the Holland Society of New York, a clue to its pride in Dutch roots.

Barr writes in rich period style, with Dutch names, customs, and speech lending color to a tale of courtship and choice. The orange ribbon of the title marks loyalty and love in a city of mixed peoples. Fans of historic romance will find a warm, old-fashioned New York tale with a strong local flavor.
18052-medoline-selwyn-s-work:
Mrs. J. J. Colter wrote Medoline Selwyn's Work in Boston in 1889, printed by Ira Bradley and Company. The book opens with a verse on the golden hour that comes but once, and it urges the reader to seize it when fortune smiles and duty points the way.

Chapters follow Medoline through Mrs. Blake, Oaklands, a funeral, a new skill learned, city life, and new friends. She works, learns, and helps, with a brave heart and a firm will. Colter writes earnest, moral fiction for young women, in the style of the day. It is a gentle tale of duty, work, and a young woman's rise.
18185-the-danger-mark:
Robert W. Chambers wrote The Danger Mark in 1909, with pictures by A. B. Wenzell, dedicated to John Carrington Yates. Chambers, a famed novelist of society and romance, here gives the Seagraves, a grand household undone by pride and passion.

The tale opens on a Sunday when fifteen servants cannot manage the house after Kathleen Severn's sudden departure. A telegram calls young Mrs. Severn to Staten Island, and trouble brews. Chapters run from the threshold and the year of discretion to confession, dusk, and the love of the gods. It is a lush, old society novel, full of scandal and style.
18513-jesus-of-nazareth-a-biography-by-j:
John Mark wrote this biography of Jesus of Nazareth, published by D. Appleton in New York and London in 1922. The book tells the gospel story in sixteen chapters, from Galilee to resurrection, in plain narrative prose for general readers. Chapter titles sum each stage of the life.

Chapters give hail, the Galilean, and a teacher with authority. They give a brother to all who do God's will, the wisdom of the ages, lord of life and love, and Is not he the carpenter. Later chapters bring thou art the Christ and strong son of God. They give master of men but servant of all, and conflict with scribes and Pharisees. Jerusalem that killeth the prophets, despised and rejected, and crucified, dead and buried close the story. The last chapter tells of resurrection. Readers get the life of Jesus as biography: teaching, conflict, death, and rising, told in order.
18655-the-cruise-of-the-noah-s-ark:
David Cory wrote this children's fantasy at New York in 1922 with Grosset and Dunlap, part of his Little Journeys to Happy Land. Its heroine, Marjorie, tires of copybook letters and sighs over her Noah's Ark toy. Suddenly Mr. Noah steps out and warns that rain will fall for forty days and nights, urging her aboard before the nursery floods.

Marjorie climbs aboard with her rag doll Maria Jane and a toy auto, as water pours over the sill. Later chapters bring a circus, a man overboard, fire, repairs, an iceberg, a thrilling rescue, a leak, a picnic, and a storm. Cory writes with warmth and whimsy for young readers.
19707-one-wonderful-night-a-romance-of-n:
One Wonderful Night calls itself a romance of New York. Its early pages picture wealth in the millions and a police chief honored at a banquet. A half million a year buys the bliss the scene describes. New York romance novels of this era loved that scale. Money, society, and one compressed night drive the form.

The single-night frame is the book's real device. Everything must change between dusk and dawn. That pressure suits romance, where a meeting can remake a life. The city supplies speed, crowds, and bright rooms. Readers of the time bought such stories as escape. The novel is a sample of popular New York romance before the pulp era.
20107-denmark:
Denmark, in this travel account, opens with its capital city, Copenhagen. The city is large and thriving, with all the marks of a trade capital. It has a mood of friendliness and gaiety all its own. English visitors, the book says, feel at home in merry Copenhagen at once.

From the capital, such accounts move to towns, coasts, and Danish customs. Readers of the era wanted clear facts mixed with warm local color. The book gives them streets, people, and scenes in a brisk tour. It serves now as a snapshot of Denmark as foreign guests then saw it.
20546-the-hand-in-the-dark:
The Hand in the Dark, published in 1920, is a mystery novel built around an old house with a violent past. The house was rebuilt by the freebooter who had burnt it down. That man, Philip Heredith, traced his line to a knight in the Domesday Book.

His ancestor's name stands among the knights of Duke William's army, which gathered at Dives before the Norman Conquest. With nine centuries of blood behind its walls, the house is ripe for secrets. The novel mixes that deep past with a modern crime, in the country-house mystery style of its day.
20556-lamarck-the-founder-of-evolution-h:
Alpheus S. Packard wrote this life of Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, the French naturalist who taught evolution before Darwin. Packard, himself a zoologist, gathered Lamarck's story and his writings on organic evolution. Lamarck's own country, he argues, never forgot him.

His countrymen called the author of the Flore Française the French Linnaeus. The writer of the great work on invertebrate animals took at once the highest rank as the leading zoologist of his period. Yet Lamarck died poor and blind. Packard's book presses his claim as the true founder of the evolution idea.
20776-encyclopedia-of-needlework:
Colour and cloth choices open the Encyclopedia of Needlework, a vast guide to hand work. Notes by each plate help readers pick shades and threads with ease. Most patterns were worked in D.M.C. cottons, praised here as the best of their kind.

Stitch by stitch, the book covers embroidery, lace, crochet, knitting, and more. Therese de Dillmont built this guide from years of teaching and design. It became the standard needlework book in homes across Europe and America. Crafters still raid its plates for classic patterns, proof of how clear and full its teaching remains.
21052-the-pirate-shark:
A serious lad in a smudgy mechanic's cap and greasy overalls fronts The Pirate Shark. Keen grey eyes, a firm chin, and straight black hair mark him a worker. An onlooker might judge him a stubborn fighter if need arose, the text adds.

H. Bedford-Jones and W. C. Tuttle fill this tale with ships, sharks, and sea peril. A young mechanic's grit meets a pirate threat on wild waters. Pulp pace rules each chapter, with peril and pluck in fast turns. The book is a brisk fossil of magazine adventure, when a boy with a wrench could stand between a ship and its doom.
22000-kept-in-the-dark:
A kept secret poisons a marriage in Anthony Trollope's Kept in the Dark, his last novel, published in 1882. Cecilia Holt lives happily at Exeter with her widowed mother, in a house with a garden, a brougham, and two boys to tend it. An early engagement to the worthless Sir Francis Geraldine ends, and Mr. Western offers her a second chance. What all her friends said about it fills a chapter, as Trollope's titles like to do.

Cecilia does not tell her new husband about the old engagement, and what is kept in the dark works its harm. Miss Altifiorla, the tale's sharp guest, stirs every pot she touches. Trollope died during the serial run in Good Words. Even unfinished in the public eye, the novel shows his fairness and his lifelong theme: pride and concealment in love.
22646-the-hunters-of-the-ozark:
Edward S. Ellis wrote The Hunters of the Ozark, a frontier adventure for boys published in 1887. Ellis was one of the most prolific dime novelists in America, and his tales of the border country taught generations of boys their idea of the wild West. The Ozark hills of Missouri and Arkansas give this one its ground.

One autumn day, Terence Clark urges his friend Frederick Linden to hunt for a cow missing since the night before. With his mother's consent, Frederick joins, and the search becomes the most eventful the two lads had ever known. Lost stock leads to wild country and wilder company, as Ellis's formula promised. The book is a clean specimen of the nineteenth-century juvenile frontier tale.
22731-tin-types-taken-in-the-streets-of-:
Tin Types Taken in the Streets of New York is a collection of character sketches of metropolitan life, issued by O. M. Dunham. The catalog record gives no year. Tin types were cheap photographs, and the title promises the verbal equivalent: quick, sharp portraits of the New York types a walker meets daily.

The sample describes one unforgettable nose. It is sharp, thin, hanging, and exceedingly ample. It comes inquiringly out of its owner's face, as if the other features had hired it as a picket sentinel. Such comic physiognomy fills the sketches, which range over newsboys, sharpers, clerks, and cranks. Books of street types were a nineteenth-century staple, half humor and half social survey. This one preserves the city's crowd as its wits saw it.
23113-to-my-younger-brethren-chapters-on:
Handley Moule closes To My Younger Brethren with an envoi on holiness. Reviewing his chapters, Moule lands on one closing thought. A ministry works rightly only through the minister's personal holiness, he writes. Not a shape pressed from outside, but a life growing outward into action.

Moule, Bishop of Durham, addressed these chapters on pastoral life and work to younger clergy. Preaching, visiting, study, and prayer get practical counsel from a scholar-bishop who had trained ministers himself. The tone is earnest and fatherly throughout. The book survives as a window into Anglican ministry at its Victorian-Edwardian height, when character was held to be the clergy's first credential.
23780-a-little-girl-in-old-new-york:
Amanda M. Douglas published A Little Girl in Old New York in 1896, dedicating it to Dorothy Moore, a little girl of today. Its heroine is a small girl whose father asks her, with jolly blue eyes in a twinkle, how she would like to go to New York to live.

Chapters follow her good-by to an old home, fine feathers for the little wren, and a first look at old New York. She meets Miss Dolly Beekman and Miss Lois, hears of sixty years ago, and joins a real party and a merry Christmas. Douglas gives young readers a child's-eye view of a city already full of old landmarks.
24220-the-tyranny-of-the-dark:
Hamlin Garland wrote this novel of psychical matters, published by Harper and Brothers in London and New York in May 1905. Its first book opens with a setting, a maid on a mountainside, a man, a second meeting, pupil and master, the Marshall Basin, the forces of light and darkness, Dr. Britt's explanations, and Anthony Clarke, evangel, with his wooing.

The second book turns to modernists, news of Viola, a patron of psychics, Kate's visit to Viola, a sleeping sibyl, Kate's interrogation, Viola's plea for help, and a telegram from Morton. Garland weighs belief, fraud, and feeling around a young medium. Readers get a period novel of séances, science, and the dark that tyrannizes minds.
24544-desk-and-debit-or-the-catastrophes:
Oliver Optic, the pen name of William T. Adams, wrote this boys' book, published at Boston in 1871 with fourteen illustrations. It belongs to his Upward and Onward series. Its hero is a young clerk, and its subtitle promises the catastrophes of a clerk: the mishaps, scrapes, and blunders of a boy learning business.

Optic, author of the Army and Navy stories and the Boat-Club stories, wrote for boys who liked work, pluck, and adventure in ordinary life. His clerk learns honesty, care, and courage through small disasters. Young readers get a cheerful, old-fashioned tale of a boy making his way in a counting-house.
2482-new-york:
James Fenimore Cooper's New York is a historical tale of the city in its early days, when Dutch and English settlers shaped Manhattan's streets and politics. The story follows the growth of the town through its families, its trade, and its conflicts, with Cooper's eye for place and custom. The city itself is the subject.

The tale belongs to Cooper's lesser-known historical fiction, written with affection for his home state. Its period detail rewards patient readers. New York history buffs will find a curious early portrait. Cooper wrote the tale as part of his effort to record New York's Dutch past.
24841-friendly-visiting-among-the-poor-a:
Mary E. Richmond, general secretary of the Charity Organization Society of Baltimore, published this handbook in 1899, reprinted in 1907. It trains charity visitors to help poor families wisely, not just with alms. Chapters take up the breadwinner, the homemaker, children, health, spending and saving, recreation, and relief.

Richmond stresses personal influence over preaching: study a child's gifts, use evening classes and clubs, and help boys and girls learn hand and brain together. Her voice is practical and humane, rooted in house-to-house work. The book remains a founding text of social work, and a clear window into how reformers of 1900 thought about poverty.
2512-the-cruise-of-the-snark:
Jack London's Cruise of the Snark recounts his attempted voyage around the world in a small yacht, from California through Hawaii to the Solomon Islands. The book mixes sailing adventure with essays on surfing, leprosy, and the peoples of the Pacific, all in London's vigorous prose. Illness and bad luck cut the voyage short, but the account remains thrilling.

The volume shows London as traveler and journalist, not just novelist. Its Pacific chapters are vivid and humane. Adventure readers will find a classic of sea travel. London built the Snark himself, at great cost, for the voyage.
2522-a-dark-night-s-work:
Elizabeth Gaskell sets this short novel in the small county town of Hamley, where Mr. Wilkins, the leading attorney for miles around, rules his home with pride and a quick temper. His daughter Ellinor loves him dearly, and her quiet life with her father and her suitor Ralph seems settled and safe.

One dark night changes everything, when a violent act by Wilkins binds father and daughter to a secret they must carry for years. Gaskell follows Ellinor as guilt, love, and fear pull her in different directions. The story is short but tense, and it asks how long one hidden deed can shape honest lives.
25274-rollo-at-work:
Jacob Abbott's Rollo at Work, subtitled The Way to Be Industrious, is one of the Rollo Books for young children. A notice to parents promises that the stories will train thinking powers and advance reading, while entertaining little readers with Rollo's doings.

Rollo and his friend James join Jonas, the hired man, to fetch cows and fill a quagmire, learning that little boys must follow directions rather than work their own way. The wood-pile lesson still stings Rollo's memory. Abbott's plain tales made industry, obedience, and observation into pleasant adventures for generations of children.
25371-northern-travel-summer-and-winter-:
Bayard Taylor's Northern Travel, published in New York in 1859, gives summer and winter pictures of Sweden, Denmark, and Lapland. Taylor states his aim plainly: his object is artistic and pictorial, not scientific, statistical, or politico-economical.

He adopts the people's way of life wherever he travels, coloring sketches with native tints and atmosphere. A Norrland inn proves as comfortable as most Stockholm hotels, at half the price, though Stockholm claims to be Sweden's Paris. Taylor's travel prose made Northern Europe vivid for American readers. Taylor traveled widely, and his Northern pictures rank among his best.
2569-the-day-s-work:
Rudyard Kipling gathers stories of work in this volume, from a bridge builder in India to a ship finding herself at sea. Findlayson of the Public Works endures three years of heat to raise his bridge, while engineers, soldiers, and sailors test themselves against machines, rivers, and war.

The Tomb of His Ancestors, The Maltese Cat, and The Brushwood Boy mix empire adventure with dreams and boyhood wonder. Kipling writes with pride in craft and duty, and his prose drives like an engine. The book remains a stirring record of the men and women who built, sailed, and fought for a world in motion.
25827-leslie-ross-or-fond-of-a-lark:
Charles Bruce, author of My Beautiful Home, writes Leslie Ross, or Fond of a Lark, published in Edinburgh by William P. Nimmo in 1871. Leslie, an only child with kind parents and a happy home, centres his parents' love and care, and once had a baby sister he remembers kissing.

Chapters ask why Leslie was sent to school, introduce Ascot House, and follow pea shooting, a linchpin, a memorable holiday, and one Ned. A flood closes the early run, as a schoolboy fond of larks and pranks learns lessons in fun, trouble, and friendship in a Victorian boys' school story.
25915-james-lane-allen-a-sketch-of-his-l:
Printed by Macmillan with a portrait, this sketch traces the life and work of James Lane Allen, novelist of Kentucky. It praises The Choir Invisible first as a love story, then as history, for its faithful picture of early Kentucky settlement. Allen's power to show the mighty stream of migration spreading through the Alleghanies into the unknown West gave his books their solid place in American letters.

The sketch ranks Allen among the foremost American writers, and ventures that no novel since The Scarlet Letter touched quite the same note of greatness. Beauty of thought and beauty of phrase burn as one fire in his work, the sketch says, in a quiet and eternal frenzy that marks the great artist. Readers get a short, warm guide to a writer of place and passion.
26120-chats-on-old-lace-and-needlework:
Mrs. Lowes's volume in the Books for Collectors series chats about old lace and needlework for buyers and keepers. It joins companion chats on china, furniture, prints, costume, miniatures, earthenware, autographs, pewter, and stamps, each with frontispiece and many illustrations.

History opens the talk: queens under Ethelred and Canute designed and embroidered church vestments and altar cloths, and Editha, wife of Edward the Confessor, embroidered the king's coronation mantle. The Bayeux tapestry, Lowes notes, is miscalled, since it is embroidery, worked by Queen Matilda to show her husband's mighty deeds. The book values old needlecraft as both art and historic document.
26134-the-last-twelve-verses-of-the-gosp:
John W. Burgon's 1871 study defends the last twelve verses of the Gospel according to St. Mark against recent critical objectors. Dedicated to Sir Roundell Palmer, it opens with President Routh's advice to verify references, and prints facsimiles of Codex Aleph and Codex L.

Burgon's chapters argue that the hostile verdict of critics is quite recent, that the early fathers bear favorable witness, and that early versions yield unfaltering testimony to the verses. An alleged hostile witness among the fathers, he claims, is an imagination of the critics, while manuscript testimony runs overwhelmingly in the verses' favor. The book is a full-dress case for genuineness.
26653-up-the-baltic-or-young-america-in-:
William T. Adams, writing as Oliver Optic, published this schoolboy travel book with Lee and Shepard at Boston in 1875, first in the second series of Young America Abroad. It records the Academy Squadron's second voyage to Europe, in the waters of Norway, Sweden, and Denmark, and Adams says he spent much of the previous year abroad gathering material. He dedicates it to Shepard K. Mattison, met at Trollhättan on the Göta Canal.

Geography, history, and politics are woven into the story, with manners and customs described for young readers. The young gentlemen visit ports, canals, and capitals while keeping academy discipline afloat. Adams promises matter as full and correct as a story could carry, in a series that had already taken young America to Ireland, England, Holland, France, and Germany.
26775-lewis-and-clark-meriwether-lewis-a:
William R. Lighton wrote this short life of the two captains who led the 1804–1806 trek from the mouth of the Missouri to the mouth of the Columbia. Its opening chapter stresses how little is known of their private lives, since both men merged themselves in their work and left almost no personal anecdotes behind. Lighton leans on the sketch Thomas Jefferson wrote at Monticello in 1813, since Jefferson had known Lewis as a neighbor and later made him his private secretary.

Thirteen chapters follow the pair from their commission and start through councils with the Sioux. They cross the Continental Divide, winter on the Pacific coast, and take the long road home. The closing chapters cover their return, their later lives, and the fame that fused their names into one joint style.
27168-the-faith-doctor-a-story-of-new-yo:
Edward Eggleston's The Faith Doctor, a story of New York in its third edition of 1891, takes mind-cure, faith-cure, and Christian science as its motive. Eggleston, who knew New York life intimately, insists his purpose is artistic, not polemical: a study of human nature under modern conditions.

The chapters follow the origin of a man of fashion, the evolution of a society man, and the Bank of Manhadoes, among others. In one age men cure by potable gold and witches, Eggleston notes, and in another by animal magnetism and aerial therapeutics, each age finding its own delusions.
2739-more-letters-of-charles-darwin-volu:
Charles Darwin's letters open this first volume, edited by Francis Darwin and A. C. Seward, as a record of his work in hitherto unpublished letters. Biographical footnotes for the set appear at the end of volume two, while editors' notes stand in the text in brackets.

The early letters trace Darwin's growth from a young naturalist to the author of a theory that remade biology. Friends, mentors, and fellow collectors crowd the pages with questions and encouragement. The volume gives readers Darwin in his own voice, curious, cautious, and endlessly observant.
2740-more-letters-of-charles-darwin-volu:
Charles Darwin's letters continue in this second volume, edited by Francis Darwin and A. C. Seward, as a record of his work in hitherto unpublished letters. Biographical footnotes for both volumes appear at the end of this volume, while editors' notes stand in the text in brackets.

The letters show Darwin at work, testing ideas, answering critics, and sharing findings with friends. They humanize the author of the Origin, revealing doubt, humor, and patience. The volume serves as a companion to his published books, and a portrait of science done by post.
27585-hilaire-belloc-the-man-and-his-wor:
C. Creighton Mandell and Edward Shanks wrote this study of Hilaire Belloc, the man and his work, with an introduction by G. K. Chesterton. Methuen published it in London in 1916, and Chesterton dedicates his introduction to H. L. Hutton of Merchant Taylors' School.

Belloc's works listed at the front include Paris, Marie Antoinette, Emmanuel Burden, Merchant, Hills and the Sea, and On Nothing, On Everything, and On Something. Chesterton recalls meeting Belloc in low spirits, noisier and livelier than anyone else's high spirits. Belloc talked into the night and left a glowing track of good things. Chesterton calls him the man who fought hardest for good things in his time.
27999-dante-his-times-and-his-work:
Arthur John Butler, late fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge, published Dante: His Times and His Work with Macmillan in 1902. Butler, who also translated Dante's Purgatory, Paradise, and Hell, writes for students facing two difficulties: the quantity already written on Dante, and the quantity remaining to be written.

Chapters also cover the thirteenth century, Guelfs and Ghibellines, Dante's early days, Florentine affairs to his exile, the exile itself, the Commedia, and the minor works, with appendices for beginners. The book remains a solid English introduction to Dante's life, age, and poem.
28549-a-treatise-on-foreign-teas-abstrac:
A Treatise on Foreign Teas abstracts an ingenious work titled An Essay on the Nerves, and warns against India tea. The writer traces health to the state of the nerves, then argues that foreign tea corrupts liquids with corrosive acids and stagnates them with obtuse alkalies. Mineral waters, coffee, and chocolate earn observations along the way, but tea takes the blame.

India tea, the faculty agree, acts as a slow poison on the nerves and the body's solids, the treatise says. Dr. Solander's Sanative English Tea, made of native and exotic plants, is offered instead, in packets at two shillings and ninepence. Readers get an eighteenth-century health scare, complete with advertisement.
29489-herbert-hoover-the-man-and-his-wor:
Vernon Kellogg's 1920 life of Herbert Hoover, printed by D. Appleton and Company, follows Hoover from childhood and boyhood through university, mining engineering, and work in China, London, and the wider world. Later chapters cover the war years, when Hoover's relief work made his name known across Europe. Kellogg, who knew the relief effort at first hand, writes with warmth and close detail.

One scene stands out: crowds in Warsaw gather to see a man whose name they all knew, though his face and voice were new to them. The book presents Hoover as a plain, able organizer raised to sudden fame by service. Readers of American lives and wartime relief history will find a vivid, contemporary portrait from just before Hoover's presidency.
29666-hymns-and-hymnwriters-of-denmark:
J. C. Aaberg traces Danish church song from its early roots to the writers who shaped it. The volume was printed in 1945 for the Danish Evangelical Lutheran Church in America. He opens with song under Catholic rule, when Latin ruled the service and Danish had almost no church books. Then he follows the Reformation, which put psalms and hymns into the tongue people spoke at home.

Three men take the main stage. Thomas Kingo's psalm book set the tone for a whole age. Hans Adolph Brorson was the pietist singer. Grundtvig, the lone defender of the Bible, became a great hymn writer. Short lives, close readings of key hymns, and a final round of lesser writers fill out the tale.
30230-a-story-of-the-red-cross-glimpses-:
Clara Barton, founder of the American National Red Cross and its president from 1881 to 1904, tells her field work in her own voice. Appleton published the New York volume in June 1904, with a frontispiece from St. Petersburg in July 1902 showing decorations given by the Czar and the Empress Dowager. Barton opens with her rule: she lived much she never wrote, but wrote nothing she never lived.

Chapters move from early history in 1880 to 1884 through the Texas famine, the Mount Vernon cyclone, yellow fever in Florida, and the Johnstown flood. Later work covers the Russian famine, Sea Island relief, Armenian relief, Cuba in 1898, and Galveston in 1900. A little girl of ten asks what the Red Cross is, and Barton's answer becomes a plain, first-hand record of relief.
30676-primary-handwork:
Ella Victoria Dobbs writes Primary Handwork, a Macmillan school book with an HTML version offering original illustrations, presenting handwork for young pupils in the primary grades. Macmillan publishes it in New York, Boston, Chicago, Dallas, Atlanta, and San Francisco, with Macmillan and Company in London, Bombay, Calcutta, and Melbourne.

Transcriber notes mark italics with underscores and bold face with equal signs, preserving the textbook's visual cues in plain text. Primary handwork teaches children to make, cut, fold, and build with their hands, linking craft to learning. The book serves teachers and pupils who value practical, creative work in the early school years.
30678-supplement-to-punch-16th-december-:
A Punch supplement dated 16 December 1914 gathers the magazine's Unspeakable Turk cartoons and captions into a single survey of Ottoman misrule. An early cartoon, The Status Quo, dated 9 September 1876, shows Turkey asking Britannia to befriend it, while Britannia refuses, pointing to hands of that colour.

England indignantly protests Turkish atrocities in Bulgaria, the supplement notes, and a later cartoon, One Bubble More, dated 6 January 1877, mocks illusory promises of reform. Everybody's Friend, dated 2 March 1878, notes German neutrality in the Russo-Turkish War and Germany's new friendship with the Turk. Punch turns decades of cartoons into a bitter historical charge.
30844-to-invade-new-york:
Irwin Lewis wrote this short science fiction tale about an invasion that need not use guns at all. Its framing idea is that in a culture dependent on machines, people grow helpless when the easy way fails, so a clever foe might strike at that dependence. The story opens in Shannon's Bar on Third Avenue, late in the afternoon, with only the narrator and the bartender Jimmy in the room.

Into the bar walks a tall, learned-looking stranger of about fifty, stooped, with tortoise-shell glasses and graying hair. He paces outside, orders a root beer by mistake, then a mild beer, and quotes Latin when Jimmy stares. Lewis builds his threat from small, odd details, not from fleets or armies. Readers get a sly, short tale about how a modern city might fall without a shot.
31602-a-canadian-bankclerk:
J. P. Buschlen's novel A Canadian Bankclerk was published at Toronto by William Briggs in 1913, with copyright in Canada the same year. It is dedicated to the conscientious clerk, and its opening verse pictures a clerk whose box is full of others' cash while his own pocket holds only air. The book follows bank life from inside the cage.

Its first chapter, Our Banker, opens in the Ontario village of Hometon at rest, where old elm trees shade the streets and a few gnarled pioneers still sigh over the new days. The second chapter turns to swipe days. Buschlen's novel traces a clerk's working life in a small Canadian town bank.
31717-the-witches-of-new-york:
Q. K. Philander Doesticks, P.B., published The Witches of New York, as encountered by himself, at New York with Rudd and Carleton in 1859. It was entered in 1858. His preface promises what New York City's witches told him themselves, without the slightest exaggeration or perversion. It shows an honest wish to report plainly on the people he met while gathering his material.

His chapters are explanatory first, then turn to the glorification of Madame Prewster, with strange things and marvellous performances, and on to Mrs. Pugh of South First Street and a full account of an interview. Doesticks's book is a satirical tour of fortune tellers and mediums, told with a humorist's eye for humbug.
31994-the-forests-of-mount-rainier-natio:
The Forests of Mount Rainier National Park was issued by the Department of the Interior in 1916 and sold for twenty cents by the Superintendent of Documents. It describes the trees and forests of the Washington park. It belongs to a series of park publications that also include d Flett's Features of the Flora, with descriptions of flowering trees and shrubs, and Matthes's Mount Rainier and Its Glaciers.

The pamphlet serves visitors and students who want to know what grows where on the mountain's slopes, from lowland forest to alpine timberline. Readers get a concise government guide, illustrated and practical, from the early years of the national park system.
32440-dave-dawson-at-dunkirk:
R. Sidney Bowen's war adventure, copyrighted in 1941, follows Dave Dawson through the early Second World War toward Dunkirk. The story opens in a Paris hotel room, the Hotel de Ney. Dave wakes staring at a combination clock and calendar, trying to recall why he placed it where he would see it first. That small mystery gives way to war: Hitler gives the order, diving doom follows, and Dave meets Freddy Farmer.

Chapters carry Dave through prisoners of war, an enemy camp, escape, a desperate mission, and trapped war skies. Bombs for Namur, orders from headquarters, Belgium giving up, and thunder in the west lead to wings of doom and the white cliffs. Bowen writes fast, patriotic air adventure for young readers, with comradeship and nerve at its centre.
32638-in-the-dark:
Ronal Kayser tells a horror tale through the dictaphone of Asa Gregg, president of the Gregg Chemical Company. Gregg sits alone in his dark office, waiting out the watchman's rounds, to leave a record for his wife. His secretary Mary Carruthers has run the firm for years, and Gregg must trust her with the message.

What Gregg confesses concerns a vat of acid in his plant and a corpse that will not stay dead. Grave-mold shaped itself into bones, then hair, then flesh, before his eyes. Acid cannot kill her, he says, and no cemented lid can hold her. The tale ends in dread, not in release.
44-the-song-of-the-lark:
Willa Cather's 1915 novel follows a Colorado girl with a rare singing gift. The Song of the Lark traces Thea Kronborg from childhood in Moonstone to the opera stage. Friends, teachers, and small-town life shape her long climb.

Six parts carry Thea through lessons, work, love, and hard choices about art. Cather sets music against prairie towns, Chicago rooms, and desert canyons. The novel asks what talent costs and what it repays. It remains a key portrait of an artist's growth. Critics rank it among Cather's finest studies of talent, work, and the price of art.
5009-the-unspeakable-perk:
Samuel Hopkins Adams's Unspeakable Perk opens with a young man who has taken on a large contract. He hates a wide stretch of Caribbean Sea. It lies very blue, still, and indifferent to human feeling. Each day he sits in the shade of an overhanging boulder. Cool air and cool water trickle down the slope. He despises the placid ocean and wishes it would dry up so he could walk home.

In plain American terms, the young man is homesick, stranded, and furious at his exile. Adams turns that comic hatred into a romance and adventure of the tropics. Readers get a witty tale of a man at odds with paradise, learning that the sea he hates may be the least of his troubles.
5142-graustark:
George Barr McCutcheon's romance begins with Grenfall Lorry, a bored American traveller boarding an eastbound train at Denver. On the journey he meets strangers who draw him toward the small European principality of Graustark, where a princess, a throne, and a plot against the crown await him.

Lorry's adventure moves from railway coaches to castles, abductions, midnight flights, and a tower imprisonment, as love and loyalty pull him into Graustark's politics. The book founded a whole genre of imaginary-kingdom romance, and it remains a brisk, escapist tale for readers who enjoy Ruritanian adventure.
6353-the-prince-of-graustark:
George Barr McCutcheon, author of Graustark and Beverly of Graustark, opens this 1914 romance with Mr. and Mrs. Blithers discussing matrimony. Mr. Blithers, fingers in his ears, conquers argument by shutting out opposition, for it is easier to express himself with ears closed than open. His wife talks for two or three minutes, then subsides in despair, for a woman will not talk to a stone wall, and he counts the discussion won.

Two countries discuss marriage, Mr. Blithers goes visiting, and Prince Robin is asked to stand up, with a letter from Maud and a voyage aboard the Jupiter. The prince meets Miss Guile, wireless messages pass through Totten's hands, and R. Schmidt reads them in a luxurious parlour. McCutcheon writes Ruritanian romance with humour, as American bluntness meets Graustark royalty and love must cross rank and ocean.
6801-beverly-of-graustark:
George Barr McCutcheon sends Beverly Calhoun east of the setting sun, on the road from Balak, through the Ganlook Gates, and inside the castle walls of Graustark. A ragged retinue, an inn of hawk and raven, a royal coach, and three princes fill the early chapters. A visit, a testing of Baldos, and a shot in the darkness lie ahead. Gossip, a rose, and a proposal follow.

Beverly, in service in a Ruritanian court, must navigate love, rank, and intrigue with wit and pluck. McCutcheon writes with the gay, romantic verve of his Graustark tales. Beverly of Graustark is a sparkling, old-style romance of a make-believe kingdom.
7213-my-life-and-work:
Henry Ford tells his life and work in collaboration with Samuel Crowther, opening with a plain question: what is the idea behind it all? His chapters run from the beginning and what he learned about business through starting the real business. The secret of manufacturing and serving, getting into production, machines and men, and the terror of the machine follow.

Wages, good business, cheap making, money as master or servant, tractors, charity, railroads, and democracy and industry follow, each treated as a practical problem rather than a theory. Ford argues in the voice of a maker who trusts work, thrift, and service over finance. The book reads as a plain-spoken creed of industry.
8041-the-bible-king-james-version-book-4:
Mark's Gospel begins at once: the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, with John baptising in the wilderness. There is no birth story and no long genealogy. Jesus moves swiftly from baptism to temptation, to preaching in Galilee, healing the sick, calming storms, feeding crowds, and confronting Jerusalem's leaders, until the passion and the empty tomb. The pace is urgent, and the word immediately recurs again and again.

Mark is the shortest Gospel and probably the earliest, prized for its vivid, breathless storytelling. Its Jesus is a man of action, misunderstood even by his disciples, and its ending leaves readers to answer who he is. In the King James Version, its directness makes it the best Gospel for a first, fast reading of Jesus' life.
8071-expositions-of-holy-scripture-st-ma:
Alexander Maclaren's expositions on Mark work through the shortest Gospel passage by passage. His titles include What the Gospel Is, The Strong Forerunner and the Stronger Son, Mighty in Word and Deed. Healing and Service, Christ's Touch, Christ's Authority to Forgive, The Publicans' Friend, and The Secret of Gladness. Later sermons cover the anger and grief of Jesus, his ambassadors, and the mistakes of his foes and friends.

Maclaren reads Mark as a Gospel of action, and his sermons match that pace, short and pointed. The volume is useful for anyone preaching or studying Mark, since each exposition stands alone. It shows Victorian preaching at its most practical, turning each miracle and conflict into counsel for daily discipleship.
8268-the-world-english-bible-web-mark:
Mark, in the World English Bible, opens with the beginning of the Good News of Jesus Christ, Son of God. As written in the prophets: a messenger preparing the way, a voice crying in the wilderness to make the Lord's paths straight. John comes baptising in the wilderness, preaching repentance for forgiveness of sins, and all Judea and Jerusalem go out to him, baptised in the Jordan, confessing sins. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the Gospel moves swiftly to the cross and empty tomb.

The modern version keeps Mark's urgency, with notes on prophetic quotations and on baptism as immersion. Its plain sentences suit a first, fast reading of Jesus' life. For readers new to the Gospels, Mark here offers the shortest, most direct account, in language that never gets in the way.
8564-life-and-travels-of-mungo-park:
Mungo Park's Life and Travels, with a full narrative of subsequent adventure in Central Africa, tells the Scottish explorer's journeys into West Africa. Contents open with an introduction, and illustrations show Park passing a lion, which quietly suffered the party to pass though they were fairly within its reach. Park sought the Niger River and the city of Timbuktu.

Park, a surgeon turned explorer, wrote one of the great travel books, plain and gripping, about African kingdoms, captivity, and survival. He died on a second expedition, and later narratives complete his story. Readers get exploration at its most personal, and a book that shaped Europe's image of Africa.
8829-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
R. F. Weymouth's Mark, in the third edition of 1913, opens with the beginning of the good news of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Isaiah's promise of a messenger preparing the Lord's way. John the Baptizer appears in the desert, proclaiming a baptism of the penitent for forgiveness of sins. People of all classes from Judaea and Jerusalem confess their sins and are baptized in the Jordan. John wears camel's hair and lives roughly, in Mark's brisk manner.

Weymouth's modern speech keeps Mark's pace: short scenes, urgent movement, healings, parables, and conflict with religious leaders, driving toward the Passion. The translation, first published in 1909, favours clarity over majesty, and it suits readers who want Mark's action without archaic diction. This single-book volume lets a reader follow the shortest gospel straight through in Weymouth's plain English.
9571-snow-bound-and-other-poems-part-4-f:
Part four of volume two of Whittier's works leads with Snow-Bound, his beloved winter idyll of the family homestead. The poem recalls his father, mother, brother, sisters, uncle, aunt, and the schoolmaster who boarded with them. Harriet Livermore, the half-welcome guest, adds fire to the fireside scenes. Snow shuts the house in, and tales fill the long nights.

Other poems in the part include My Triumph, In School-Days, My Birthday, and Red Riding-Hood, with A Legacy and Abram Morrison beside. Whittier writes of home with warmth and exact recall. A reader gets his most cherished fireside poem, plus short lyrics of youth and age, in one gathering.
9579-songs-of-labor-and-reform-part-5-fr:
Part five of volume three of Whittier's works gathers his Songs of Labor and Reform. The Quaker of the Olden Time opens, praising a calm, firm man unspotted by his age's wrongs. Democracy, Seed-Time and Harvest, and To the Reformers of England follow. Songs of Labor then salute shoemakers, fishermen, lumbermen, ship-builders, drovers, and huskers in turn.

Later pieces take in a Brussels peace meeting, a prisoner for debt, and the poor voter on election day, with disarmament and Italy's freedom beside. Whittier honors toil and peace with equal warmth. A reader gets reform verse of breadth and heart, where work itself becomes a hymn.
9585-at-sundown-and-other-poems-part-5-f:
Part five of volume four of Whittier's works centers on At Sundown, his late poems of age and memory. At Sundown opens, addressed to a poet friend, with winter grass and arbutus under snow as signs of hope. The Christmas of 1888, The Vow of Washington, and The Captain's Well follow. Tributes to Holmes on his eightieth birthday and to James Russell Lowell add warmth.

Later poems mark Haverhill's 250 years, honor Milton and Sigourney, and watch the wind of March and the last eve of summer. Whittier, old and honored, writes with calm and grace. A reader gets a poet's sundown verse, gentle and luminous, from a life near its close.
a-dark-night-s-work:
Elizabeth Gaskell opens in Hamley, a small county town, where Mr. Wilkins the attorney dines with the gentry his family has served for three generations. His son Edward inherits the practice and the standing, and marries a woman above the family's habits. One dark night, a quarrel in the Wilkins household ends in a killing.

The rest of the novella follows the hiding of that night's work and the long weight it lays on Edward and on Dixon, the loyal servant who shares the secret. A daughter grows up under its shadow. Gaskell, writing in the 1896 collection used here, turns a crime story into a study of guilt eating a respectable life from inside.
after-dark:
Wilkie Collins strings his short tales on a single thread in this collection, as his preface explains. The frame is Leah's diary: Leah is the wife of a traveling portrait painter who is losing his sight. While he rests his eyes, friends and sitters tell stories, which Leah writes down to earn money.

The tales between the diary entries run to mystery, crime, and strange adventure, each with its own prologue from the painter. Ghostly warnings, hidden identities, and narrow escapes fill the pages. Collins, a master of suspense, built the frame with real care, so the frame story itself, about art, poverty, and a wife's devotion, holds its own beside the tales.
beverly-of-graustark:
George Barr McCutcheon's Beverly of Graustark is a Ruritanian romance set in the imaginary mountain principality of Graustark, east of the setting sun. The contents promise an inn of the hawk and raven, a castle, a royal coach, three princes, a testing of Baldos, and a boy who disappears.

Beverly Calhoun, the American heroine, travels the road from Balak through the Ganlook Gates and inside the castle walls, amid gossip, proposals, shots in the darkness and a grotto's secrets. McCutcheon writes in the high-spirited, romantic manner that made Graustark famous among readers of light adventure. Anyone who enjoys imaginary kingdoms, dashing princes and plucky heroines will find Beverly pure entertainment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-the-:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Park Abbey describes a Norbertine house half a mile south of Louvain. Duke Godfrey Barbatus founded it in 1129. He owned an immense park there and invited the Norbertines to a small church he had built. Walter, Abbot of St. Martin's at Laon, brought a colony of canons and led them for nearly three years.

Once numerous enough, the canons elected Simon of Laon as abbot, and they ministered across the Louvain district, reclaiming those seduced by Tanchelin's errors. In 1137 the abbot founded the Abbey of Our Lady and Sts. Cornelius and Cyprian at Ninove, and Godfrey made Park's abbots his arch-chaplains. Philip, Simon's successor, grew the buildings and readied the soil for farming, while Blessed Rabado's devotion to the Passion marked the house's piety.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o:
The old Danish diocese of Aarhus took in Aarhus and Randers provinces, Samso and Tuno islands, and, after 1396, part of Viborg. About 900, King Frode of Jutland raised the Holy Trinity church at Aarhus. Hamburg's Archbishop Adaldag consecrated Reginbrand as missionary bishop in 948, and when Reginbrand died in 988, all Jutland merged into a single diocese centred on Ribe or Viborg.

A fresh division came in 1060, with Christian ordained as Aarhus bishop. Ulfketil, bishop from 1102 to 1134, planned the town, while Svend Udsson, bishop from 1166 to 1191, founded the Cistercian abbey at Om. Peter Vagnsen started Saint Clement's Cathedral in 1201, close to the wooden church Ulfketil had built for Clement's relics. Gifts at Prince Niels's tomb, where he was buried about 1150, helped pay for the stone cathedral, finished about 1263 and largely burned in 1330. Later bishops raised the fine building standing today, and the last Catholic bishop, Ove Bilde, was imprisoned in 1536.

Roskilde stood suffragan to Hamburg from about 991 to 1104, then to Lund until 1536. Its diocese took in Zealand and Moen, with Rugen in Pomerania. About 960 King Harold Bluetooth built a wooden church to the Holy Trinity at his new capital, Roskilde. Its first bishops were Godebald and Gerbrand, both Englishmen, and Aage.

Bishop William began the first stone cathedral. Svend Norbagge finished it in 1080 with King Saint Canute's help and enlarged its chapter to fifteen prebendaries. Svend also completed the Benedictine abbey of Ringsted. Under Arnold, a nobleman led a movement against clerical marriage, and the skull of Pope Saint Lucius I reached the cathedral, whose patron he became. Later glories include the abbeys of Soroe, Ringsted, and Skovkloster, the five-towered church at Kallundborg, and the intact Carmelite priory at Elsinore, home of Paulus Helgesen.

Viborg, in Denmark, covered the province of Viborg, the town of Aalborg, and lands in Aalborg and Randers, the Randers hundreds passing to Aarhus in 1396. The diocese was founded in 1065, after the death of Bishop Vale. Herbert was its first bishop, from 1065 to about 1100, and in 1080 Saint Canute endowed bishopric and chapter, the latter Canons Regular of Saint Augustine.

Bishop Svend I, from 1106 to 1112, drowned in the Elbe at the Count of Stade's hands. Eskild, from 1112 to 1133, began rebuilding the cathedral about 1130. He was murdered during Matins in Saint Margaret's church by order of King Eric Emun. Svend II ruled from 1135 to 1151. Niels I, from 1153 to 1191, gave generously to his chapter. He founded Saint Michael's hospital in 1159 and the Cistercian nunnery of Asmild in 1169. He finished the original Romanesque cathedral, of which only the crypt remains. He secured Kjeld's beatification and the translation of his body to its shrine.

York held metropolitan rule in the north, though its Christian origins are unknown. Bishops sat there from very early times, but the line breaks before the later archbishops. Eborus of York attended Arles in 314. York bishops also attended Nicaea, Sardica, and Ariminum. Pagan Saxons wiped out the early community, leaving only legendary names: Sampson, Pyramus, and Theodicus.

When Gregory sent Augustine to convert the Saxons, he planned archbishoprics at Canterbury and York, each with twelve suffragans, but the plan failed. Paulinus, consecrated in 625, received the pallium in 631, yet held no suffragans. His successors went without the pallium until Egbert in 732. After Paulinus fled in 633, the country fell back into paganism. Celtic bishops from Lindisfarne converted it anew, but York had no bishop again until Wilfrid in 664. The article lists archbishops from Thomas of Bayeux and Thurstan to Walter de Grey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-meinw:
Meinwerk, tenth Bishop of Paderborn, rebuilt his ruined diocese into a center of building, learning, and parish life. Born to the Saxon Immedinger family, he was educated at Halberstadt and Hildesheim. He served as chaplain to Otto III before Henry II named him bishop in 1009 to rescue the impoverished see.

Over twenty-seven years he rebuilt the fire-damaged cathedral, consecrated in 1015. He founded Abdinghof Abbey in 1031 and a collegiate church at Bussdorf. He raised city walls and an episcopal palace, and divided the diocese into parishes. He also revived the cathedral school with teachers of mathematics and astronomy, and improved farming for his people's material welfare, dying in 1036.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cork:
Patrick Sexton's entry covers Cork, Corcagia, Corcagiensis, in Ireland, suffragan of Cashel. Saint Finbarr founded the see and served as its first bishop. Born about the sixth century's middle at Rathculleen, six miles north of Bandon, and educated in Leinster, he spent time on a Gougane Barra island. He then founded a monastery and school at Lough Eirc, the marshy Lee expansion under the city. City and diocese take the name Cork from corcagh, marsh.

The monastery rose on a plateau south of the city, now the Rock, close by the Protestant bishop's palace. Students soon flocked thither, rapidly taking the large marsh island beneath, building there and giving birth to a city now numbering over 70,000. At the Reformation, Bishop Bennett lost the see's temporalities in 1535, and remaining churches passed to Protestants. In 1430, at Cloyne's bishop's instance, Cork and Cloyne united, remaining so until 1747. The 1891 census counted 178,461 Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-denmark:
A country survey of Denmark as it stood when the encyclopedia was written, covering land, faith, politics, letters, and art. Jutland and islands such as Zealand and Fünen form the kingdom, with the Faroes, Iceland, Greenland, and three West Indian islands attached. Former reach had been far wider, taking in southern Swedish provinces, Schleswig and Holstein, and Norway.

Religious history opens with early missions, including a failed visit by Archbishop Ebbo in 823. Political history starts with ice sheets and ends with a modern state, while literary pages note rune stones, Viking chronicles, and later writers. Art sections trace wooden churches, stone cathedrals, carved altars, and frescoes, with the painter Abildgaard among the artists named.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-egbert-archbi:
Egbert was Archbishop of York in the eighth century, dead on 19 November 766, with his birth date unknown. Son of Eata, he was brother of King Eadbert of Northumbria. He was cousin of King Ceolwulf, to whom Bede dedicated his history. He was schooled in a monastery and ordained deacon at Rome with his brother Ecgred. Ecgred died at Rome, and Egbert came home.

Named Bishop of York in 732 on the resignation of Wilfrid II, he took Bede's long letter of advice to heart. Bede urged more priests, prayer and study, the Creed and Lord's Prayer in Saxon, and smaller dioceses for steadier visits. In 735 Egbert won the pallium from Gregory III and became the second Archbishop of York, ruling the northern bishops as suffragans. His pupil Alcuin praised his piety, energy, and gentle sternness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ethelbert-arc:
Ethelbert was Archbishop of York, England, date of birth uncertain, dead on 8 November 781 or 782. His name also appears as Albert, Adalberht, and Eadberht. He was teacher and intimate friend of Alcuin, whose poem on York's saints and prelates is the principal source for his life. He was a kinsman of his predecessor Egbert and a pupil in the school Egbert founded at York.

On reaching manhood, he was ordained priest by Egbert and made master of the school. Among his pupils was Alcuin, who described his varied erudition: grammar, rhetoric, law, poetry, astronomy, natural history, and Sacred Scripture. Accounts call him severe to the stubborn and gentle to the docile. His sympathy won his students' affection, and his energy urged them on. Even after Egbert became archbishop, he kept the New Testament lectures, entrusting the Old Testament to Ethelbert.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerard-archbi:
Gerard, Archbishop of York, fought Canterbury for primacy and died disgraced in 1108. Nephew of Walkelin of Winchester and Simon of Ely, he began as precentor at Rouen cathedral and clerk in William Rufus's chapel, which sent him to the pope in 1095. Rewarded with Hereford, he was consecrated by Saint Anselm on June 8, 1096, having been ordained deacon and priest the day before.

Made York's archbishop on Henry I's accession, Gerard claimed equal primacy with Canterbury and refused profession of obedience to Anselm. Sent to Rome over investitures, he claimed private assurances the decrees would sleep, a claim pope and Anselm's monks denied, and he stood excommunicated until confession. He later professed obedience yet asserted York's independence. Reforming York, charged with immorality, avarice, and magic, he died suddenly without sacraments, and canons refused him cathedral burial while crowds stoned his hearse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gospel-of-mar:
The Gospel of Mark is the Second Gospel, chiefly on Christ's Galilean ministry and the last week at Jerusalem. After a brief introduction on the Precursor, the Baptism, and the temptation, the body covers the public ministry, Passion, Death, and Resurrection. A Catholic Encyclopedia article treats its contents, authorship, language, text, place and date, purpose, and relation to Matthew and Luke.

Mark passes in silence over the infancy events of the other Synoptists. He cares far more for Christ's acts than his discourses, only two of which run at any length. Miracles are told most graphically and fill almost a fourth of the Gospel, 164 verses out of 677 in the Vulgate. They impress readers from the outset with Christ's power over all nature. The body falls into Galilee, Judea and Peraea with the journey to Jerusalem, and the last week.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gurk:
Carinthia's prince-bishopric of Gurk, suffragan of Salzburg, was erected in 1070 with the backing of Alexander II and Henry IV, and its first bishop, Günther von Krapffeld, took office in 1072. Salzburg's archbishop kept appointment, consecration, and investiture at first, the chapter won election rights under Roman I, and a 1535 pact split nomination between sovereign and archbishop.

Grown from a small territory to the whole of Carinthia by 1859, with its residence moved to Klagenfurt in 1787, the diocese counted 369,000 Catholics in 1906 across 345 parishes. Benedictines at St. Paul's, Jesuits, Dominicans, and other orders fill its institutions, its cathedral at Gurk dates to about 1220, and Maria Saal draws 15,000 to 20,000 pilgrims a year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jesuit-s-bark:
Jesuit's Bark, also called China bark, cinchona, or Peruvian bark, is the famed remedy for malaria drawn from cinchona trees of the western Andes. Its alkaloids made it the most celebrated specific against every form of the fever, and its story shaped pharmacy, botany, medicine, trade, and tropical farming.

Once the bark itself was dosed in many forms; today its alkaloids are made in bulk, chiefly in Germany, from plantations in Java, Ceylon, and farther India. Physicians long praised it above Spanish gold and silver, and Ramazzini likened its advent to gunpowder's for war. Two hundred eighty years of use confirm a drug that changed how fever was fought.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-clerk:
John Clerk was a bishop and diplomatist who served Cardinal Wolsey and Henry VIII through the divorce crisis. Educated at Cambridge and Bologna, where he became doctor of laws, he attached himself to Wolsey. He gathered preferments: rector of several parishes, Dean of Windsor, judge in Star Chamber, and Master of the Rolls from 1522 to 1523.

As ambassador to the papal court he presented Henry's book against Luther to the pope before the full consistory and acted as Wolsey's agent in two conclaves. Made Bishop of Bath and Wells in 1523, he was first appointed a counsellor for Queen Katharine in the divorce. He was then persuaded to agree she withdraw from Rome proceedings, and later joined in pronouncing the divorce sentence. His last embassy, explaining Anne of Cleves' divorce in 1540, ended with illness at Dunkirk and death in England in 1541.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mary-the-moth: Mary, mother of John surnamed Mark, appears in Acts 12:12, where the church gathered in her home. From that fact we may gather she held some wealth, since her house could host the gathering. She may have been a widow, for had her husband lived, his name would likely have been given in place of hers. Beyond this single glimpse, nothing further is known of her life or work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-metalwork:
Metalwork in the Church's service covers the vessels and utensils of metal used in liturgy from the earliest days. The practice grew through the Middle Ages, when church metalwork's history was largely the history of metalworking itself. The Church was the foremost patron, nearly all surviving medieval pieces are ecclesiastical, and until the twelfth century monks and clerics made almost all goldsmiths' work.

The entry ranges from antiquity through Byzantine, barbarian, Carolingian and Othonian, Romanesque, Gothic, and Renaissance work. It centres on precious metals, though iron, bronze, and brass also served the Church richly. Even in the Renaissance, church metalwork stayed a major branch of the goldsmith's art, and today it still ranks among the crafts where that art can most profitably unfold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-new-york:
The Archdiocese of New York was erected on 8 April 1808 and made archiepiscopal on 19 July 1850. It covers Manhattan, Bronx and Richmond boroughs plus Dutchess, Orange, Putnam, Rockland and York counties, and the Bahama Islands, 4,717 square miles in New York and 4,466 in the Bahamas. The Bahamas joined in 1886, since access was easiest from New York, after belonging to Charleston.

Its suffragans are Albany, Brooklyn, Buffalo, Ogdensburg, Rochester and Syracuse in New York, plus Newark and Trenton in New Jersey. All these formed the original diocese in 1808. Albany and Buffalo split off in 1847, Brooklyn and Newark in 1853. New York is now the largest see in population and most important in influence and prosperity among American ecclesiastical divisions. The entry traces its colonial origins, bishops, parishes and institutions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-newark:
Newark is a diocese created in 1853, suffragan of New York, covering Hudson, Passaic, Bergen, Essex, Union, Morris and Sussex counties in New Jersey, 1,699 square miles. It originally covered the whole state, but fourteen counties left in 1881 to form Trenton. As early as 1672 records show Catholics at Woodbridge and Elizabethtown, East Jersey's capital, visited by Jesuits Harvey and Gage, Governor Dongan's New York chaplains.

Later priests included Alsatians who came with Carteret for salt-making. William Douglass, elected from Bergen, was barred from the first General Assembly at Elizabethtown in 1668 for being Catholic, then arrested and banished to New England as a troublesome person. The colony's atmosphere was intensely anti-Catholic, and the 1698 toleration law expressly excluded Roman worship. West Jersey's Quaker pioneers were more tolerant. The entry follows the diocese's bishops, parishes and growth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-noah-s-ark:
Noah's Ark, the great box of Genesis, is sized and fitted out in this entry from the biblical text and later reasoning. Three hundred cubits long, fifty wide, and thirty high, it was built of cypress and sealed inside and out with pitch. Inside were three decks of rooms, one small window, and a side door God shut himself.

Trials by modern writers, the entry notes, found such a hull steady for heavy cargo and calm on waves. Inside, Noah's family, pairs of animals, and their food waited out the Flood until the vessel grounded on the mountains of Armenia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-mark:
Mark was consecrated on 18 January 336 and died on 7 October 336. After Sylvester's death he rose to Rome's bishopric. The Liber Pontificalis calls him a Roman, son of Priscus. Constantine's letter summoning bishops over the Donatist dispute is addressed to Miltiades and one Mark, evidently a Roman cleric who may be the pope himself. Both his election and death dates are historically certain.

Nothing has come down about any part he played in the East's Arian troubles. An alleged letter to Athanasius counts as a later forgery. Two constitutions bear his name. One gave Ostia's bishop the pallium and ordered that bishop to consecrate Rome's bishop, a privilege Ostia certainly held by the late fourth century, as Augustine attests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-mark:
Mark the Evangelist stands at the centre of this long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. It treats the John Mark of Acts as the same man named by Paul and Peter in their letters. Son of Mary of Jerusalem, whose house sheltered the early Church, he carried both a Jewish name, John, and the Roman name Marcus by which readers knew him.

Working through the New Testament evidence, the entry traces his ties to Barnabas, his break and later reunion with Paul, and his close link with Peter in Rome. It then weighs the old tradition that his Gospel preserves Peter's preaching, and surveys what early writers said about his later life and death. Readers looking for the scriptural case, not just the legend, will find it laid out step by step.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-of-cor:
The School of Cork won wide fame above all in the seventh and eighth centuries. Its name comes from corcagh, a marsh, since Lee floods once covered the low ground where most of modern Cork now stands. Its founder, Barra or Bairre, called Finbarr the Fair-haired, gives the school its story. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a brassworker's son to sainthood.

Barra's family belonged to the Hy Brinin Ratha of Galway's eastern shore. His father, a skilled brassworker, moved to Hy Liathain in west Cork, where the saint was born about the mid-sixth century. His chief teacher MacCuirp, or Curporius, had himself studied under Gregory the Great at Rome. To perfect himself Barra withdrew to a hermitage on a lonely island in the lake still called Gougane Barra, and his school grew from that solitude.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-ch:
The Sisters of Charity of Saint Vincent de Paul of New York began in 1817. Mother Seton sent Sister Rose White, Cecilia O'Conway, and Elizabeth Boyle from Emmitsburg to found a community in New York. The mother-house stands at Mount Saint Vincent on the Hudson. The community must not be confused with an earlier congregation of the same name.

Tension grew over affiliation with the Sisters of Charity in France. Their superiors pressed changes in customs, including withdrawing sisters from boys' asylums, a move that threatened the New York orphanage. At the same time no sisters could be had from Emmitsburg for a much-needed New York hospital, now Saint Vincent's. After correspondence between Archbishop Hughes and Father Deluol, the Holy See extended Emmitsburg's privileges to the New York community on 20 June 1847.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-southwark:
Southwark was the diocese covering south London and the south-eastern counties of Kent, Surrey, and Sussex, suffragan to Westminster. This entry dates its founding to the restoration of the hierarchy in England in 1851. When the old London District, once ruled by a vicar apostolic with jurisdiction reaching to North America and the Bahamas, was divided at the Thames.

At first the new diocese also took in Berkshire, Hampshire, and the Channel Islands, and the entry follows its parishes, clergy, and institutions as London grew around it. For readers tracing English Catholic life after emancipation, Southwark's story shows a church rebuilding its organization in the heart of a fast-expanding capital.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-paulinus-a:
Paulinus, archbishop of York, brought Christianity to the Northumbrian court and then fled south with its queen. A Roman monk of St Andrew's monastery, he was sent by Gregory the Great in 601 with Mellitus to aid Augustine and carry the pallium. He worked in Kent until 625, when he escorted Ethelburga north to marry the pagan king Edwin.

Consecrated bishop before leaving, he converted Edwin, baptised on 12 April 627, and large numbers of his people. He fixed his see at York, began a stone church, and preached at Yeavering, Catterick, Dewsbury, and Southwell. After Edwin's defeat in 633 he bore the queen and her children safely to Kent. He died at Rochester on 10 October 644.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-state-of-new-:
New York State, one of Britain's thirteen colonies turned American states, is surveyed here in geography, history, and church life. On 4 July 1776 it adopted the Declaration of Independence with its sister colonies. It spans from 40 degrees 29 minutes to 45 degrees north, and from 71 degrees 51 minutes to 79 degrees 45 minutes west, covering 49,170 square miles, of which 1,550 are water.

Its physical geography runs from the Adirondacks in the north to Catskill and Blue Ridge branches of the Appalachians in the south and east. The article then traces settlement, revolution, growth, government, education, and above all the Catholic Church: dioceses, parishes, schools, colleges, and religious orders. It closes as a reference portrait of a state where Catholic life grew from a persecuted minority to a great communion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syracuse-new-:
Syracuse is a New York diocese of seven counties, covering 5,626 square miles, a little over a ninth of the state. Out of 609,041 people, about 161,000, more than a quarter, are Catholics. Its story begins with the Oneida and Onondaga peoples. Their central village on Indian Hill served as seat of government for the League of the Five Nations.

Recollect Franciscans may have said Mass on these shores as early as 1615. Le Moyne the Jesuit counts as the real founder of the local Church. Chaumonot and Dablon said Mass on the chosen site on Sunday 14 November 1654. They raised a bark chapel with Indian help under St John the Baptist. They added St Mary's of Ganantaa for French settlers. Those first missions soon faded, and local histories close the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-catholic-:
Catholic gentlemen of New York found fellowship and purpose in the club described here, defined by its constitution as men governed by devotion to the Church and fidelity to the Holy Father.
