Its objects were to advance Catholic interests, improve members morally, foster a true Catholic spirit, and encourage study of history, literature, science, and art, sustained by a library and frequent social intercourse.

Roots lay in the Xavier Alumni Sodality, organised in 1863 beside the College of Saint Francis Xavier under Father Dealy. In March 1871 members formed the Xavier Union to pursue ends beyond a purely religious body. Clubhouse, membership, and activities follow, sketching educated Catholic society in Gilded Age New York.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
San Marcos at Lima is the highest institution of learning in Peru and reputedly the oldest university in the New World. A royal decree of 12 May 1551 had Charles V grant 350 gold dollars to the Dominican priors to found an Estudio General at Lima, with all the prerogatives of Salamanca. Pope Pius V confirmed the decree by a bull dated 25 July 1571.

Until 30 December of that year the school stayed under Dominican control, then became independent with the right to elect its own rector. The first rector chosen was Dr Gaspar de Meneses, a layman. In 1574, after a new site was bought for 600 gold dollars, the name Saint Mark was adopted. The entry follows the university's faculties, colleges, and scholars through colonial and republican times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-use-of-york:
In medieval canon law it was received principle that, for judicial matters, sacraments, and the more solemn fasts, the custom of the Roman Church must be followed. Yet for church services each church kept its own traditions, as Gratian's Decretum records. So there arose a number of Uses, the special liturgical customs of a diocese or group of dioceses. In England before the Reformation the south and midlands followed the Sarum Use, while most of the north followed the Use of York.

The general features of these medieval English Uses appear fairly in the peculiarities of the Sarum Rite, which the reader may consult. The entry then sets out York's distinctive traits: its calendar, its chant, and its ceremonial differences from Sarum. It closes with the Use's fate at the Reformation, when the Book of Common Prayer replaced the old diocesan customs across England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-clark:
William Clark was an English priest executed at Winchester in 1603 after tangling with both Jesuits and the crown. His birth date is unknown. He entered Douay College in 1587, moved to the English College at Rome in 1589, took orders, and returned to England in April 1592. In the quarrel over Blackwell as archpriest, he joined thirty-three priests who appealed against Blackwell from Wisbeach Castle in November 1600.

Father Persons attacked the appellants' character, but Clement VIII backed them in October 1602 and restored their faculties, despite efforts to shut Clark out. Found saying Mass in the Clink prison, he faced closer confinement, then arrest over the shadowy Bye Plot. Nothing was proven against him beyond work for Catholic interests, yet he was condemned on 15 November and hanged a fortnight later, protesting his death as martyrdom.

govdocs-archive_org-man-and-technics-osw:
Oswald Spengler, author of The Decline of the West, published Man and Technics in 1931 as a short contribution to a philosophy of life. Its subject is technology, which Spengler treats not as a neutral tool but as the driving tactic of human existence.

He argues that technics began with the predator's way of life. It reached its peak in Faustian Western man, whose machine culture he expects to turn destructive and to spread beyond its makers' control. The book compresses Spengler's dark view of history into a few chapters. It remains his most read short work on the machine age.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIFeltWMark_FB: W. Mark Felt, once a senior FBI official, appeared on the CBS News program Face the Nation on August 29, 1976. The archived record preserves that broadcast appearance under his name. The file gives the program, the network, and the date. It gives no transcript detail in the surviving evidence. govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WeissMark_Weiss: Harold Weisberg wrote on April 28, 1983, to Barger, Aschkenasy, and Weiss about his FBI Freedom of Information lawsuits. The recipients were acoustics researchers tied to the evidence in his cases. Weisberg's suits forced many assassination files into the open. The letter shows the legal fight and the science working side by side, with experts and a litigant sharing one long campaign.
graustark:
George Barr McCutcheon's Graustark begins on an east-bound express from Denver. Grenfall Lorry, a rich young American who has hunted and fished on four continents, boards with the air of a martyr. A lady in the dark passageway changes the journey in one meeting of eyes. The train carries them toward a ship, and toward her secret.

The lady is the Princess Yetive of Graustark, a tiny principality in the eastern European mountains. Lorry follows her home, where a forced marriage to a neighbouring prince threatens her throne. Disguises, a prison cell, and a midnight rescue fill the Ruritanian plot. McCutcheon invented the pattern that a hundred romances copied: American pluck against Balkan intrigue. Graustark's success founded a series and a genre. Its princess, its mountains, and its cheerful impossibility still define the imaginary kingdom novel.
life-and-travels-of-mungo-park:
Mungo Park's travels in Africa anchor this combined life and narrative. Contents begin with what ancients and Arabs knew of the continent. Park trained as a surgeon before the African Association engaged him. His preparations and departure from the Gambia River follow.

Park reached Pisania, the British factory on the river. Sickness struck him there before he set out for the interior. Later chapters promise a full narrative of subsequent central African adventure. The book preserves the record of a famed early African explorer. Ledyard, Lucas, and Houghton precede Park among Africa's English explorers. Portuguese and English discoveries frame the introduction's survey.
making-both-ends-meet-the-income-and-out:
Making Both Ends Meet studies how New York working girls lived on their wages. Sue Ainslie Clark and Edith Wyatt wrote it for Macmillan in 1911. A photograph by Lewis Hine faces the title page. The authors dedicated the book to Florence Kelley, the reform leader.

The study grew from the Consumers' League's work on laundry labor. Laundry owners met the League to seek a ten-hour day. Clark and Wyatt record real budgets, rents, food, and carfare. Girl after girl tells how her pay falls short of her needs. The book became a classic of Progressive Era reform. It lets working women speak in their own figures.
medoline-selwyn-s-work:
Mrs. J. J. Colter wrote Medoline Selwyn's Work, held in rights in Boston in 1889. Ira Bradley and Company printed the book. A verse at the front urges readers to seize the golden hour.

Mrs. Blake and Oaklands open the tale, and Esmerelda comes third. A funeral, a new skill, and Mr. Winthrop mark the early turns. City life, humble charities, and a Christmas tree fill the middle. Mrs. Le Grande's tale and a changed heart lead toward the close. A helping hand and a pleasant surprise lift the later heads. The tale ends from the depths, after much loss and change.
more-letters-of-charles-darwin-volume-1-:
Francis Darwin and A. C. Seward edited this first volume of their father's further letters. Its subtitle calls it a record of his work in hitherto unpublished letters. The editors dedicate it to Sir Joseph Hooker, Darwin's lifelong friend. A quotation from Darwin thanks Hooker for constant kindness and encouragement.

The preface explains that the Life and Letters of 1887 left much unused. New letters arrived from correspondents including Galton, Huxley, Lyell, and Owen. The Hooker correspondence forms the chief treasure, written with complete freedom. Even Darwin's most technical letters gain personal charm there, the editors say, and this volume begins that record.
more-letters-of-charles-darwin-volume-2-:
Volume Two continues the letters of Charles Darwin edited by Francis Darwin and A. C. Seward. The biographical footnotes for both volumes are gathered at this volume's end. Its opening chapter treats geographical distribution from 1843 to 1882. The letters here run from 1867 onward.

Letter 378 is from Joseph Hooker at Kew, dated January 20, 1867. Island plants and animals, and how species spread, dominate the science of these pages. Darwin argues distribution is key evidence for evolution by natural selection. Readers watch him test the theory against facts from his botanist friend's global network, year by year, in his modest and careful voice.
my-life-and-work:
Henry Ford tells his own life and work with help from Samuel Crowther. The contents open with a bold question: what is the idea? Early chapters trace his beginnings and what he learned about business. Then comes the secret of manufacturing and serving.

Later chapters treat wages, machines and men, and cheap goods. Ford asks why not always have good business, and why be poor. Money, he argues, must be a servant, not a master. Tractors, railroads, and charity all get his plain views. V1 called it a bestseller that put his creed on record, for better and for worse.
nasa-tm-19710001808-manned-space-flight-:
NASA published this account of its Manned Space Flight Network, the chain that tracked Apollo flights. Tracking, command, and talk with the crews were Apollo's vital links with Earth. The network worked in two broad phases for each mission.

Near Earth, a worldwide chain of stations with mid-size antennas did the work. Once a craft passed ten thousand miles out, much larger antennas took over for their power and precision. The network held a dozen ground stations, one ship, and four jet aircraft. All were linked to the Mission Control Center in Houston. It had to give instant, reliable contact from liftoff to splashdown.
new-york: New York is a work by James Fenimore Cooper, the American novelist. The hosted sample holds only a Project Gutenberg header, so it preserves no readable content from the work itself. The record gives no year, and the bare title names only the place. Nothing in the sample shows whether the piece is tale, sketch, or history. Readers should treat this note as a title level guide only, and check the full text for the work's true form.
podcast-joerogan-7HoFQdKD9Rk:
Paranormal creators Sam and Colby join the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1922. The pair built a huge online following by spending nights in haunted houses and filming what happens. Rogan, a skeptic with a soft spot for ghost stories, gives them the floor.

They trade their best ghost-hunting stories, from famous haunted sites to nights that scared them off a location. Rogan asks how they rule out tricks and what they truly believe they caught. The episode is a storyteller's session: part travel log of America's spookiest places, part debate over whether anything out there answers back.
podcast-joerogan-yUsJIcqwARk:
German author Norman Ohler brings his book Blitzed to episode 2183 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Ohler researched how deeply Nazi Germany ran on drugs, from soldiers' meth to Hitler's own injections. His work changed how many readers picture the Third Reich.

Ohler explains how the stimulant Pervitin fueled the early blitzkrieg campaigns. He describes the drug culture around Hitler and his personal doctor's cocktail of shots. Rogan asks how much the highs and crashes shaped decisions that killed millions. History's dark students get a gripping, well-sourced tour of the Wehrmacht's hidden fuel.
religion-in-earnest-a-memorial-of-mrs-ma:
John Lyth wrote this memorial of his mother, Mary Lyth of York, in 1861, and signed his preface from Stetten in Württemberg. He calls the work an act of Christian duty, not of family affection alone. Her steady example and her prayers, he says, taught him as a child that religion is the one business of life.

Lyth warns that readers seeking startling incident or fine writing will find little here. His mother made no claim to learning and her story held no romance. What he offers is the growth of grace in a plain life, and proof of how much decision, plain purpose, and steady conduct can do.
snow-bound-and-other-poems-part-4-from-v:
Poems by John Greenleaf Whittier fill one part of a larger set, sorted here under nature poems, poems of self and memory, and religious poems. The contents list Snow-Bound first, then My Triumph, In School-Days, My Birthday, and Red Riding-Hood. Later heads name Response, At Eventide, Voyage of the Jettie, and My Trust, with an autograph poem and A Legacy in the next group.

Whittier gives Snow-Bound, a winter idyl, to the memory of the home it describes. His note names the folk of the Whittier homestead: father, mother, brother, two sisters, an uncle and aunt, and the district school-master who boarded with them. The half-feared, half-welcome guest, he explains, was Harriet Livermore, a young woman of fine gifts, strong temper, and fervent faith.
songs-of-labor-and-reform-part-5-from-vo: John Greenleaf Whittier's anti-slavery poems stand under the head Songs of Labor and Reform in one part of his works. The contents lead with The Quaker of the Olden Time, Democracy, and The Gallows, then Seed-Time and Harvest and To the Reformers of England.
